title: Mysterious Gas Leaks Hint Mars May Still Be Volcanically Alive
summary:
Mars may not be as dead as it looks. Mysterious puffs of gas rising from cracks near a giant Martian volcano suggest that heat and volcanic activity could still be hiding deep beneath the planet's surface.

Researchers found unusual amounts of hydrogen chloride gas above fractures on the slopes of Alba Mons, an enormous volcano. The gas kept showing up in early summer, when it normally almost disappears, and always over the same volcanic cracks. That timing and location made scientists suspect something more than ordinary air chemistry was at work.

An international team led by Alexander Trokhimovskiy thinks the gas could be coming from hot magma underground. If they are right, Mars still has volcanic systems able to release gases to the surface.

The gas was first spotted by the European Space Agency's ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, which detected hydrogen chloride in the Martian atmosphere in 2021. On Earth, this gas often escapes through openings connected to magma. 'Our findings suggest that Mars has retained enough internal heat to support volcanic activity until recently, and possibly still does,' said Daniel Mège of the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, a co-lead author of the study in Science Advances.

Close-up images from the orbiter's CaSSIS camera showed narrow fractures that look relatively fresh, some stretching hundreds of metres across the surface, with strange changes in colour around the cracks. One idea is that gases from magma deep below travel up through these fractures. On Earth, openings like these are called fumaroles.

The researchers think bitterly cold Martian winters, when temperatures can fall to minus 120°C, let ice seal the cracks shut. As temperatures rise in early summer, the ice turns straight into vapour, opening the way for underground gases to escape.

Mars is home to the largest volcanoes in the Solar System, and some erupted within the past few million years. Instruments on the surface have also recorded marsquakes. But nobody has ever directly seen a new eruption or fresh lava on Mars, so whether it is still volcanically active remains an open question.
why_it_matters: Mars is the planet humans most want to explore, and knowing whether it is still warm inside helps scientists understand how planets change and where future explorers might find heat or water.
